newsitem.title: UK: Britain battles bootleggers for Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Britain battles bootleggers for Christmas.

text.p: British customs have drafted in extra officers for a Christmas crackdown on "booze cruise" bootleggers running a multi-million pound smuggling racket.
For the trickle has turned into a flood with hundreds of "daytrip entrepreneurs" taking the ferry to France and returning in transit vans weighed down with beer, wine and tobacco.

The bootleggers earn about 2,000 pounds ($3,300) a trip, their contraband is freely available around the country and Treasury officials reckon the trade now costs Britain 770 million pounds a year in lost tax revenue.
Steve Clement, customs chief in the southern English port of Dover, tries to stem the flow with 75 officers working round the clock.
"Bootlegging is on the increase but so is our ability to deal with it. It is not growing as fast as it was. The trade is peaking," he told Reuters.
Under European Union rules, Britons are allowed to return home with hefty allowances of spirits and tobacco for their own personal use.
But the yawning tax differentials between Britain and the continent have spawned bootlegging on a giant scale.
"In Britain today, 59 per cent of all hand-rolled tobacco is bootlegged. As many as six million cigarettes come across in a single consignment," Clement said.
"Within 20 minutes of your office, I bet I could show you where you could get illegal spirits and tobacco."
Customs officers stopped almost 2,300 bootleggers last year. Detections are up 20 percent so far this year. Prison sentences average from four to six months.
Across the English Channel in the booming French port of Calais, cockney entrepreneur Dave West boasts six warehouses and an annual turnover of 30 million pounds in tobacco, wine and beer.
Bootleggers are his business and he is unrepentant. There is certainly no love lost between him and customs chief Clement.
Clement says of West: "He is facilitating crime as he is under no doubt that his goods are bootlegged.
"However there is nothing we can do or would do. He is on foreign territory and we have no jurisdiction. But he is no Robin Hood, he is not a loveable rogue.
"He has found a loophole in the law and is damaging legitimate trade in this country."
As burly, tattooed customers in dark glasses and scruffy jeans queue up at his Calais warehouse, West argues: "I am inciting people to break an unpopular law.
"We are keeping the crime rate down and taking people off the street who would be involved in petty crime. They'd be out mugging or smashing in your car window.

"The money they earn gets spent in the British economy. No one loses out. There has been no increase in Britain's drink taxes for two years. I put that down 100 percent to pressure from us. We are doing a great public service." ($1=.6003 Pound)
